explanation: Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word that has been split up, mostly ' cr' (cranked, criminologist, craves, crummy, crashing) and ' y' (y'know, yesterdays, yodeling), plus the first digit of a number split into pieces in dates and times ('[1]1.20', '[1]2 July', '[1]969'). Other word-initial fragments ((c), x86, Oxford) also fire, but more weakly.

Mixed bag. It fires strongly on the constant term after ' - ' in generated algebra problems ('- [3]68*w', '= [0]'), on the first letter inside parenthesized acronyms ('([G]-CSF', '([PS]AP', '([D]CT'), and on assorted content or function words at the end of a noun phrase ('crossover special', 'situation', 'soft'). No single shared feature.

Fires on the head noun, or the word-completing token, at the end of a fixed multi-word phrase or term whose earlier part predicts it (deadly force, diastolic, bring to the table, mental health problems, mass-to-charge, made the mistake, on line 130, HOMEDRIVE). It also fires on math subscripts like $p$. Weak on tokens that aren't predictable phrase completions.

Fires on the second digit of a four-digit year written after a month/day in a date, i.e. the '0' in '2[0]13' or the '9' in '1[9]94', and on the space before a year after 'Month day,'. It is strongest in legal, court and copyright date headers, moderate on years in running prose ('in May 2015'), and weak on other digits.

Fires mostly on the first sub-word piece of a proper name or technical term that has been split into pieces, e.g. ' Pe' in Peugeot/Pezold/Peper, ' Man' in Manawatu, ' May' in Mayawati, 'Gh[ul]am', 'AP' in APPELLATE, and chemical-name pieces like '-d'. It also fires on scattered other tokens (license-text commas, 'and', '-p'). Its strength depends on the token beginning a word the model must complete.

Fires on function or modifier words in the middle of a clause that lead into the object or complement noun phrase, especially 'from', 'other', 'another', 'outside', 'future', 'further', 'public', 'is', inside phrases about exclusion or relation to others ('barring from', 'isolated from outside influences', 'harm to other people'). The pattern is diffuse and fires on many ordinary connective tokens.

Its main moderate activity is on housing and residence words (bedroom, sq. ft, Single Family, homes, cottage, lofts, 'at home'). Its single strongest example is the exponent '2' in a LaTeX square such as a_1^{2} and b^{2}. Weaker hits fall on staying or keeping phrases ('sitting on', 'kept locked away').

Fires on tokens in biographical or encyclopedic text about sports and education, especially college or minor-league athletics: 'for' in 'played ... for California', 'league' in 'minor league', 'a' in 'As a senior', conference names (Big Ten, All-Sunshine), and school or place-name pieces ('N' in NMSU, Nauvoo). It is weaker in legal attorney listings and other bios.

Fires on many unrelated tokens: the year's last digit in Wikipedia 'Category:1988 births/deaths' tags, sports-career words ('to win its first title', 'college career', 'another year', 'final season'), code tokens ('<' in an XML dependency, '.get', ').'), and assorted phrase completions ('personal use', 'personalised service').

Fires on punctuation and small boundary tokens that close off a list item, a clause or a citation: periods ending sentences in boilerplate or disclaimers, commas and semicolons in lists of names or charges, the decimal point in measurements ('4.6 mm'), and numbers in parentheses. It also fires on some unrelated content tokens. Overall it is a loose 'segment boundary' detector.

Fires on the token that completes a highly predictable word or fixed phrase, either the final sub-word of a name or term (K[immel], Dop[pler], Fukuy[ama], counterv[ailing]) or the expected word in an idiom ('coming [to]', 'easier [said] than done', 'Where are you [from]', 'Big [Ten]', 'Bay [State]'). Tokens that are not strongly predicted by context stay weak.

Fires on the token that completes a predictable multi-token name or identifier, often a repeat of something earlier: 'New [Zealand]', '[button]Image', 'jsfiddle[.net]', 'Must[ard]' after Mustard, and the closing digit of dates or IDs in lists of years, versions and case numbers. The token is strongly predictable from local context or an earlier repeat.

Fires on the main finite verb that comes right after a subject noun phrase, especially a long or complex subject: 'statement [points]', 'column ... [states]', 'train of thought [led]', 'functions [return]', 'Volunteers ... [bring]'. This holds across English, French, Spanish and Dutch, and verb endings like 'vol[gt]' and 'reprenn[ent]' also fire.

Fires on the token right after 'do' or 'Do' when 'do' is part of a larger word or construction: 'Do[ord]ash', 'do[led] out', 'dout'orado', 'do['s] and don'ts', and, more moderately, 'Do [you]' and 'Do you [think]' questions. It also fires on the numerator or 'd' right after '\frac{' in LaTeX, and on 'di[ethyl]'.

Fires mainly on the '.' between the major and minor parts of a software version number ('2[.]0', 'Maven 3[.]6.3', 'GLEW 1[.]9', 'License-2[.]0'). It also fires on mid-word or grammatical tokens in French and Russian text (ne sach[ant], чтобы [не], получ[ается]) and on a few English tokens ('can't', 'all time').

Fires on structural punctuation and operators in code, markup or other structured text: commas and coordinates in SVG paths, '<' in class inheritance and comparisons, '[' in LaTeX theorem definitions, '/' and ':' separators, ' =' in assignments, and '|' in tables. The common thread is syntax delimiters rather than words.

Fires on the keyword that opens a control-flow statement in code, mostly ' if' at the start of an indented line (also 'else if', 'while', '.then'). It also fires on identifier pieces inside code and on some other code tokens, and stays weak outside code.

Fires on the second token of a technical compound term or set phrase, where it completes the term: Type [I] error, hypoth[al]amic, ssh[-key]gen, below [normal], [proportional] representation, tax [increment] financing, NoClassDefFound[Error], immunos[up]pressive, [extrad]ited. These come from scientific, medical, legal and code contexts.

Fires on a middle sub-word piece of a word split into several tokens, typically a rare surname, place name or technical word (Pfle[ider]er, Cou[vent], Beg[otten], th[ym]idine, pyrote[chn]ic, Herst[mon]ceux, carp[ent]ers), plus some short code identifiers (' rev', ' r'). Whole common words stay weak.

Mixture. It fires on ' carried' in 'study was carried out' (and 'may be carried out'), on ' file' in 'No such file or directory' errors, and on scattered pieces of technical identifiers or strings (PLSALGORITHMS, D/dalvikvm, amd64, p2c). There are also some disease and medical terms.

Fires on a word-piece containing the letters 'ob', 'ob'-like sequences or 'Rob' that starts or continues a name or word: Rob (Robinson, Robins, Robotic, Robes, Robo), 'ob' (wobbling, Tobii, Tobacco, Stobie), comb (combattif, combinatorial), cob, Lob, Zeb, and a 'b' after a vowel. Pieces built around a 'b' sound with a short vowel are what drive it.
